utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, before the break we saw three clips related to your speech in Borovo Selo. In the second video, you refer to the audience as offsprings of the heroes from Vucin Dol. That relates to victories of the Montenegrins won in summer 1876 against the Turks; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In these victories a huge amount of Turks were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of both Turks and Montenegrins were killed. The Turks were the occupiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And calling upon an audience in a village in which a lot of people have already been killed, in particular also Croat policemen, that sounds to me like encouraging further violence, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you might have drawn that conclusion but my conclusion is quite different to yours. I was addressing the people, the public, who until then had lived in freedom and who loved their freedom. Now, the participants of the Vucin Dol battle were Montenegrins who had fought for their freedom, and that's how I saw the peaceful inhabitants of Borovo Selo who rose up, quite simply, against those who had come armed to impose their power upon them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the third video clip that we saw, you compare the policies of the Croatian leadership with, as you said, "the frenzied Croatian ideology from 50 years ago." That does not calm down the situation in that hot spot; right? It rather does the different.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had not everything resembled the policy of Hitler's Croatian state, Pavelic's state of 50 years ago, then probably the inhabitants of Borovo Selo wouldn't have behaved that way during those days. But everything that was happening during those days at that time very vividly reminded the Serb population of Borovo Selo to what happened to the Serbs 50 years earlier, and that is what disturbed them, and that is what made them organise themselves and put up resistance, because up until those days, that population was a peaceful population. The people lived in their houses, they tilled their fields, and then suddenly they were faced with a situation where they felt themselves to be under threat, under jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in that third speech you also refer to the suffering of the Serb people. Mr. Kostic, non-Serb inhabitants in Borovo Selo suffered, too, didn't they? But you don't refer to them. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right on that score, but I should like to ask you, in view of the fact that 15 years have passed since then and that we saw the clips just four days ago, may we just show -- see that third clip to remind ourselves of it for me to be able to answer you and to see on the basis of what you draw your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I don't think we need to see the clip again, but I can quote -- I can quote from the transcript that I have here in front of me, and I was actually referring to the following that what you said -- pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, to be fair to the witness, we'll see the clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As for the AV booth, we do it on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we to have a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The volume was down. We cannot hear the soundtrack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you start again so we can have a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In addition he said that we have a revamping of the ideology that was started 50 years ago. Europe and the world remembered that policy very well, and I'm convinced that Europe and the world will finally understand it today as well, come to realise what the policy and politics meant and what consequences such a policy can have, not only on the Serb people living in this area of Croatia, who is most directly in jeopardy, but also the consequences that such a policy could have further afield in Europe as well. Our federal organs, especially the Federal Executive Council, up until now have not been on a par with their job, because due to force of circumstance, we are dealing with an area in jeopardy where the Serb people are suffering, and it is the concern of the Federal Executive Council in this case and in all other cases to be expressed fully and materially viewed regardless of the ethnic composition of the population which that unfortunate situation has engulfed. We'll do everything in our power to see that that Yugoslav People's Army of ours, which is strong and mighty and which has the wherewithal to act even more than before to offer its assistance and support to all parts of the population who are jeopardised or who have already been jeopardised, regardless of where they reside, where they are. Today it is the Serb people in Croatia that are under threat. Now, if future developments take the course none of us would like to see, I don't exclude the possibility of certain other parts or other ethnic groups find themselves in jeopardy in certain areas as well. Then our army must be the force to act. It must be truly a popular national army that will stand up to protect each and every citizen under jeopardy regardless of which ethnic group it belongs to or which religion or which political options."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's enough. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That was the third clip that I was referring to, Mr. Kostic, and as I hear you here, you are referring to the suffering of the Serb people of Borovo Selo and not to the suffering of the non-Serb people of Borovo Selo. And my question to you was why do you refer only to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't think you understood the sense of what I said properly, and that is why I asked that it be played again. I spoke, and a moment ago, before we actually saw the clip, I repeated this, that the Serb people on the territory of Croatia during World War II, that is to say 50 years previously, experienced a terrible genocide. Over 700.000 Serbs, Jews and Gypsies were on the execution sites of Jasenica and others in World War II on the territory of Croatia. And so when I spoke of the suffering --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Jasenovac, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when I spoke of suffering, I was speaking about the suffering due to the same forces and the same ideology that had raised its ugly head again. So it was in that sense that I spoke about the suffering of the Serb people. But I'm fully conscious of the fact that with the situation as it was, and when we talked about it 14 years ago Croatian policemen were killed, Serbs were killed. Wherever you have weapons, wherever you have guns, then it is quite clear, especially if you're dealing with an inter-ethnic clash, that there will be casualties. The result the mistrust on both sides and the terrible experience of the past. There must be victims, and I am very sorry for each and every victim that falls.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we saw Goran Hadzic sitting next to you in that video just played. Mr. Hadzic, he was a close associate of Jovica Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic; right? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I met Mr. Hadzic for the first time on that occasion when I visited Borovo Selo. When I visited Borovo Selo. Now, whether and to what extent Mr. Hadzic cooperated with Mr. Stanisic, whom I don't personally know nor did I ever have occasion to meet him, I don't know, or with anybody else. I know that I met Mr. Goran Hadzic later on, during the long meetings when the entire leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina had a 40-hour long meeting and then several other meetings that lasted five or six hours when we tried to persuade them to accept the Vance Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, do you know that Mr. Hadzic closely cooperated with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw Arkan myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you know that he was stationed in Erdut, do you? Do you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I learnt about that, or I heard about that later on, that his forces were there, and when I attended these proceedings, actually, when I followed this trial, but at the time I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you were in Borovo Selo, you did not just visit refugee camps, you also visited the barricades; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I didn't say barracks. I said barricades, the barricades that were put up by the people at the entries of the village.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't visit any barricades either. We crossed the Danube River on -- on a raft because it was impossible to communicate via the bridge. And to tell you the truth, I don't know the area very well, so I don't know whether the river flows upstream or downstream at that particular point where we crossed in the raft. But I do know that there were paramilitaries positioned all around, Croatian paramilitaries, that they had mortars, and I also know that in crossing the river in the raft, in crossing the Danube, we could have been under threat and the target of mortars of the Croatian paramilitaries. And that is why instead of the time announced when we would cross the Danube, we crossed two hours later on the raft. But we didn't visit any barricades at all, nor did I notice any barricades, for that matter, in crossing from the embankment to Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic -- and also I would like to put a translation of a Tanjug domestic service report to the witness. We only have the English translation of this report. We don't have the B/C/S version of this Tanjug report. It's from the 29th of July, 1991, referring to your visit in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question? That is to say I owe Mr. Bonomy an answer about -- to a question about the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I was just going to ask you, shall I take this opportunity to answer that question now while that is being set up, or shall we leave it 'til later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We'll have your response at the end of the cross-examination. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, this article is actually -- or, rather, this Tanjug report is actually quoting you, and it is very much like the clip that we saw, but on the last line in this report, it says: "Kostic also went on a tour of the defenders of Borovo Selo and the barricades at the entry of this village." That is what is written here by Tanjug domestic service. Can you comment on this? They say here that you visited the defenders of Borovo Selo and the barricades at the entry of this village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What do you say to that, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that Tanjug's information at that time was mostly correct, and from that point of view as far as any information coming out of Tanjug, I had no criticisms to make. I think that everything that happened in Borovo Selo was recorded in the three clips shown by the Prosecution. So I visited the inhabitants of Borovo Selo, I went to the centre of Borovo Selo, and the welcome there, the address I made and the talk to the leaders of the Serb people in the area, you've seen all that. But I don't know where the barricades were. I don't recall seeing any barricades. Perhaps I passed by them without knowing they were there. And even if I had visited or toured the barricades, I don't see anything bad in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 945.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when you visited the village and you spoke to the people there, did you notice that it was not just local Serbs but also Serbs from Serbia there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I was in the area for the first time. I'd never been there before. And you asked me a moment ago about Arkan and about Mr. Stanisic. They were - how shall I put this? - well, let me say well-known figures, but I never met them. Now, how I could have recognised somebody and known they were from Serbia proper or from Borovo Selo, I don't know. All I could do was to recognise the people who came in the delegation with me, and amongst them there was Mr. Brana Crncevic, as you were able to see, but I said he didn't come there as a writer but he went there as a man in charge of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask the question. Mr. Kostic, your visit to Borovo Selo was understood by the Croats and also by others as endorsement of the killing of the Croat policeman. Was that said about your visit? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, I assume you talked to the Croats over there, but on the basis of everything I stated publicly and on the basis of the tape of my speech that you showed here, neither the Croats nor anybody else could have understood it that I was lending my support to someone while coming out against someone else. I stated quite clearly, and I can repeat it again, that at this point in time and in that case it was a matter of the Serbs being jeopardised on the territory of Borovo Selo, but in other cases, in other instances, what could easily happen was that the Muslims, Albanians, Macedonians and Croats might be mentioned - I don't know if I mentioned all of them - but in all events we with our Yugoslav People's Army, which is truly a people's army, will stand up in protection of anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I simply asked you whether your visit in Borovo Selo was understood by others as an endorsement of the killing of Croat policemen, and I ask you this because you yourself mentioned that this visit to Borovo Selo was the reason why Mr. Mesic did not accept you as the head of the monitoring mission. So he, at least, understood it this way, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, you would have to ask Mr. Mesic that. Mr. Mesic, at The Hague conference, told me when I had visited the units of the Yugoslav People's Army at Dubrovnik, told me, "Ah, so that's it, Branko, you're visiting the Chetniks around Dubrovnik." And there was nothing else left for me but to tell him, "No, Stipe, I'm not visiting the Chetniks. I'm visiting the members of the Yugoslav People's Army, the sole legitimate armed force in this country, of which you are the supreme commander but unfortunately you are not performing your duty pursuant to the constitution, so I had to do it instead of you." So if you gained that conclusion on the basis of what Mr. Mesic said, I myself didn't arrive at that conclusion, nor was my visit turned against anybody. My visit took place to mitigate the suffering and pain of that unfortunate jeopardised people of which 8.000 had already crossed the river Danube and fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we -- Mr. Nikola Samardzic testified in this court in the Prosecution case, and he also referred and said, "Borovo Selo was understood as endorsement of the murder of the Croat policemen for the Serb cause." He refers to your visit in Borovo Selo. And it's Exhibit 339, page 7, Your Honours. He also mentioned that this was understood as an endorsement of what had happened in the past there. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it was not my intention to mention that individual, because he -- he is dead. We say never speak ill of the dead. But since you mention Mr. Samardzic, I did follow these entire proceedings, this whole trial, and I have to say that the most -- or the ugliest assessment of the situation was made by Mr. Samardzic, because in his testimony, the only thing that he said correctly was in that portion of his testimony when he said that I asked that he be replaced. Well, you must allow me to answer your question and to complete my line of -- train of thought. If you've referred to Mr. Samardzic, then let me say what I think about Mr. Samardzic, because you are drawing conclusions on the basis of his testimony now. So the only thing that I am going to say is that Mr. Samardzic, the only thing that he said during his testimony was that at that time I called upon the responsible people in Montenegro to replace him because he was occupying the post of the minister of foreign affairs in Montenegro and he wasn't serving his people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let me interrupt you again. I would like to move on, and I would like to put to you a quote from your book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness omitted to say the only thing that Samardzic did say in the course of his testimony, but he said the only thing he said correctly was that he asked to be replaced. Everything else was not correctly stated by Samardzic, but the transcript seems to say differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. That's noted. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put now a quote from your book or, rather, a letter that you mention in your book to you. That's Exhibit D33, tab 72, and it is on page 265. Can it be provided? Mr. Kostic, it is --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, it's a letter by a group of 40 professors of your university, the Podgorica University, and they say the following: "It is no credit to us that our university does not lag behind in the slightest with a number of teachers and fellows who propagate violence and hatred from prominent positions within the ruling and other political parties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought it would have been provided.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not it. That's not the portion you read out. It's not there. It's not page 265.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please read from what actually was provided to you. It was -- at least in the version of the book that I have, it's page 265.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last paragraph, the one that is marked, it says: "In the second part of the 10th Extraordinary Congress held --" but this is not it -- "when the League of Communists changed its name into the Democratic Party of Socialists --" this is not it. You want to quote something else, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I was actually referring to this letter, this letter from the university, the colleagues from the university of Titograd, and I think you have it in your book; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S that is attached to the translation you have is obviously not the correct one. We will change that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But luckily you have --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The English version is correct. The English is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. What page, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the second page, in the middle, I started to read. "It is no credit to us that our university does not lag behind --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "-- in the slightest with the number of teachers and fellows who propagate violence and hatred from prominent positions within the ruling and other political parties. "A special place among them belongs to Dr. Branko Kostic, vice-president of the country's non-existing Presidency, who considerably contributes to the disintegration. Dr. Kostic's controversial political activities in the past three years, beginning with his recommendation to save the bullets for the coming war and a street brawl and signing up to become a volunteer in the army to the scandalous statements at the Conference in The Hague ..." Mr. Kostic, first of all my question is: Did you actually say "Save the bullets for the coming war," and what was the location?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one occasion at large rally, which was attended by over 700.000 [as interpreted] people as was assessed, when there was a shooting incident and people were sitting up in the trees in clusters, and others were firing into the air. I wanted to keep control over the rally, so I said to the seething crowd, "Keep your bullets. Don't waste them." And I have to say that after that not a single shot was fired. What I said has been used and abused, very often by people who do not share my opinions. At a rally which I did not organise but which was organised by a political party led at the time by a person who is still a persona non grata in Sarajevo, who was unfortunately a colleague and professor of mine at the university and who changed his opinions more than once, he quoted this under the title "Organiser from the background." I will tell you exactly on which page of my book it is all explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you had an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That was the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Mr. Robinson, it's page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- No, Mr. Kostic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Again another -- Could that please be admitted, Your Honour? And it's actually the B/C/S version would be page 270, not as said here, 265. It's actually following, when you look into the batch, little batch that you have, it's following in the B/C/S, it's attached here just a few pages later. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what about the reference to a street brawl?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say the following in this connection: At the time I was president of the Presidency of Montenegro. This happened in June. We were supposed to be celebrating the anniversary of the so-called Belvedere demonstrations of 1937, when there was bloodshed. The regime of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia shot into a crowd of peaceful demonstrators. Several people were killed or wounded. My father was also seriously wounded then. Even without regard to my post as president of the Presidency of Montenegro, I felt duty-bound to attend because of my family. Mr. Momir Bulatovic was also there. We met in the municipal building of Cetinje municipality before leaving for the ceremony. In front of the Cetinje monastery there was an event that had been organised. A group of young men who were being rowdy and causing a disturbance had been brought in to the police station. Their supporters then organised themselves and arrived in front of the Assembly building. There were about 20 or 30 of them in a group, and they arrived at the moment when I was leaving the building. I was in the building and I was president of the Presidency, so I should have been informed of this, but unfortunately none of the security personnel informed me. I didn't know that a group of young men had been arrested, nor did I know that another group was moving towards the building in an organised manner. Although there were some 20 or 30 policemen there, this group walked up to me. I didn't know what this was about. Of course I could have avoided them, but I met them to see what this was about. They were shouting, "Let our comrades go, let our comrades go. Release them." I didn't know what this was about. One of the young men in the group, who was in the second or third row and was taller than all the others, said, "You are a traitor of Montenegro. You are selling Montenegro." And he spat at me. This whole group was surprised by his action. They moved back a few metres, and my security men advised me to withdraw to the Assembly building, the Municipal Assembly building. Cetinje is my town, and I was ashamed. Not that someone was spitting at me as president of the state, but that someone should be treating me in this way. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic. That's -- is that your account of the street brawl? Did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to say this. I was angry and confused. I walked towards the group, and I kicked the young man who had spat at me in the lower part of his body. The police then moved the young men 20 or 30 metres off, and from there they continued yelling. I didn't want to take refuge in the Municipal Assembly building but waited for the situation to calm down. Once everything was under control, I walked towards the group to see what this was all about, because I still didn't know why they had gathered. As I was walking towards them, they started yelling, "Throw away the pistol. Throw away the pistol." It was summertime. I unbuttoned my jacket. It was light jacket. I opened it, and I said, "I have no pistol. I don't need a pistol in my town of Cetinje." And they yelled, "And the policemen behind you?" I turned around and I really saw a group of policemen following me. I ordered them to go back, and they obeyed. I approached the group, a small group, because in the meantime my driver had pulled me back. This young man was bleeding. He had been hurt and some young man had taken him across the street. I had quite a normal conversation with some of these young then. They addressed, "Comrade Branko, this was not intended for you." We had quite a normal conversation. I later went to attend the ceremony, but people still remember the misinterpretation that I was actually taking my jacket off in order to start fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the end of the account now, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just one more question. You said that the demonstrators said, "You are selling Montenegro." What did you mean? Selling Montenegro to whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can draw your own conclusion, but it's quite clear to me why you're asking me that. That's why I asked Mr. Bonomy not to be angry at with me at one point in time. You see Mr. Bulatovic in his book talking about our disagreements about the legal status of Montenegro and the future state, accused me of siding with Mr. Milosevic. Because of these accusations constantly hurled at me, even by my party comrades, I kept repeating that I was not siding with anyone, that nobody loved Montenegro more than me, and that my concern was for the future of my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have answered my question. It's no need to go in so many details. Try to answer my questions as short as possible so that we can finish the cross-examination as soon as possible. Mr. Kostic, another -- another chapter in your book --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, your questions are malicious. That's why I have to be more extensive in my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The questions are not malicious. They are, in fact, quite appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, another section in your book, and I would like to refer you now to the pages 217 starting. And I would like to have the translation provided to everyone in the court and the document also for Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Kostic, it's actually a speech, a rally on the 2nd of October, 1990, and I think that's the rally that you just spoke about with the 700.000 people attending. Is that the speech that you refer to in your book?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, all of Montenegro doesn't have 700.000 people in it. I said 70.000 people. That's the rally. And thank you for drawing attention to this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. A little bit -- on page 3 in the English, the second paragraph. And it should be marked, actually, for you. You see the following -- you said the following: "The looming tragedy in this country, the looming tragedy of the Serbian people in Croatia is too great for us to divide ourselves into parties and sympathisers. Serbian children and Serbian women and the helpless elderly are fleeing their homes again, once more they are forced to seek help or salvation in military barracks." Mr. Kostic, you gave this speech on the 2nd of October, 1990. That is a little bit later than the so-called log revolution where certain barricades were set up. What you are talking about, Serbian children, Serbian women and the elderly having to flee, that hadn't happened then, had it? How can you say those things?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about Borovo Selo, it hadn't happened. Borovo Selo happened only in 1991, and this was in May. I visited it in June. I was, however, referring to what was happening in the territory of Republika Srpska Krajina, Knin, Benkovac, and other places in Croatia inhabited by Serbs. And it was already evident. The media were already reporting that Serbian people, women and children, were trying to take refuge, inter alia, in JNA barracks. Inter-ethnic tensions and conflicts did not start in 1991, but the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In 1990, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were already attacks on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kostic, we are hearing evidence now for quite some time, and the first violent clashes we hear about is actually Plitvice and Pakrac. That's all in 1991. But here in 1990, you speak about Serbian women and Serbian children fleeing, and the elderly. That's an extraordinary exaggeration. Wouldn't you say that? Isn't it? That didn't really happen at that time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this rally, which an opposition party attempted to organise and the aim of which was evidently to win me over for that party, as they told me later, but of course they didn't succeed, this whole rally was organised in order to calm down tensions, not to exaggerate. What is certain and beyond dispute is that in the municipalities in the Knin-Krajina, where the Serbian population was in the minority and where large-scale ethnic conflicts had not yet broken out where the JNA was not engaged and where the police forces of the Tudjman government had not attempted to entered and disarm the police on the territory of the Serb municipalities, there was uncertainty, and there certainly was fleeing by the Serb population, and there certainly were helpless people seeking refuge in JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic. Mr. Kostic, in that same page -- or, rather, in your book you refer to that event as an atmosphere, indeed inferno, singing slogans, banners, calls for taking up arms, and in such an atmosphere you speak of the Serbian children and Serbian women being threatened. And you also speak about the genocide threatening the Serbian people in Croatia. That's actually fuelling the wave of nationalism and what was going on there. That's fuelling the wave, isn't it? It's adding to the tension, not calming.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, madam. You can draw your own conclusion, but if you read my book carefully, you will see, and this is perhaps one of the things that brought me to the post of president of the Presidency in Montenegro, I'm referring to the fact that at that time when ethnic passions were already seething, I was the one putting out the flames in Montenegro, calming down the passions of the crowd, and getting the crowds to disperse peacefully. This happened at this rally as well as the rallies in Rozaje and Plav, where only Muslims and Albanians had gathered on one side, and Serbs and Montenegrins on the other, separated only by a police cordon. And they couldn't be made to disperse throughout the day, and at the end of the day, when I arrived, I managed to get the crowd to disperse peacefully, thus avoiding bloodshed. All my efforts at the time, madam, were aimed at calming the tensions and not fanning the flames, but you can draw your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you already spoke with Mr. Milosevic about the Ohrid peace declaration and it's actually at page transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just reminded, I would like to tender that speech -- that part of the book, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Ohrid peace declaration testimony part, Your Honour, is at transcript 47819 to 47820. In relation to the Ohrid peace declaration, that's tab -- that was Defence Exhibit D333, tab 20, there is also, on page 2, but I think it's enough that I read it to you, it's actually said that: "The Presidency will form a state commission to determine the facts of the situation and examine the implementation of the peace declaration. In this declaration there's also mention that it will be requested that the European Community Monitor Mission would participate."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you remember that? It's actually on page 2 in the English, the third paragraph. It says here: "The SFRY Presidency will form a state commission to determine facts of the situation and examine the implementation of the decision, and it will request the European Community Monitoring Mission to participate in monitoring the execution of these decisions." However, Mr. Kostic, do you recall that you had a meeting with Mr. Jovic and Mr. Milosevic on the 2nd of August, 1991, regarding that issue and where you decided to not allow the European observers to participate? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the Ohrid Declaration very well and also the entire Ohrid meeting. You omitted to mention that the Ohrid meeting was concluded unsuccessfully. It was broken up by Franjo Tudjman, who walked out of the session before we had adopted the Ohrid Declaration. In spite of this, the rest of us who remained adopted the Ohrid Declaration. Stjepan Mesic insisted that the JNA withdraw to its barracks. The rest of us did not agree to this. The rest of us wanted the JNA to withdraw after the disarming of the paramilitary formations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards your specific question, I'm just coming to it. I was just about to answer your question. With respect to this meeting with Jovic and Milosevic on the 2nd of August, as you say, I really don't remember it. I can, however, confirm that from the very first day we had reservations with respect to the internationalisation of the Yugoslav crisis. We were doing everything not to internationalise it. Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Mesic, Mr. Ante Markovic, and the minister of the interior, Mr. Loncar, were doing everything to internationalise the Yugoslav crisis. Therefore, I do not exclude this possibility. I really don't remember this meeting, but it's possible I attended some such meeting and that I expressed reservations towards the engagement of the European Community in the solving of our crisis. Later developments proved me to be right, because the international community took a very one-sided approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you must endeavour to answer the questions more directly and more briefly than you have been. Just get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was actually referring to Mr. Jovic's testimony and his book, "The Last Days of the SFRY," entry 2nd August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, during your testimony you spoke about two visits of a delegation from Western Slavonia that saw you - and that's at transcript 47642 - and you said that the army did not have enough resources to protect the people in Western Slavonia. Mr. Kostic, my question in this regard is: You are aware that Seselj's volunteers and the White Eagles came to Western Slavonia, in particular Ploce, and did engage in clashes there. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither with respect to Seselj's men nor with respect to the White Eagles did I know anything about this at the time. I know that Seselj's men were in the area of Western Slavonia when the Serbs who fled from Western Slavonia asked me to address them in the trade union hall in December, if I'm correct, 1991. And on that occasion Mr. Seselj called me on the telephone to ask me whether he could also attend this rally of refugee Serbs from Western Slavonia, because he said that he had volunteers whom he had sent there. I have already said that I was informed that Seselj sent volunteers but that he did not organise them as separate units; rather, he sent them to join the JNA and the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you spent quite some time with Mr. Milosevic on the wording of the Brioni Declaration, and it was Defence Exhibit D333, tab 68, and you both agreed that there was no mentioning of the three-month suspension on the independence declaration, and you -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: However, among the documents related to the Brioni Declaration, there is also a memorandum of understanding on the monitor mission to Yugoslavia of 13th July, 1991. Do you know about this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please remind me what this is about. Was it an annex to the Brioni Declaration or is it a different document? Because with respect to the Brioni Declaration, I already said that we didn't have a meeting of the Presidency at Brioni. Mr. Jovic and I went there and came back, but no meeting of the Presidency was held. It was only the presidents from the secessionist republics and representatives of Croatia and Slovenia that attended. The Brioni Declaration was accepted only later by the Presidency and by the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the Brioni Declaration, there is an Annex II that refers to monitor mission, and what is now put to you is a memorandum of understanding of the working of the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Annex II, the guidelines for the mission in Yugoslavia, the monitor mission in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I do not refer to Annex II. I refer to the memorandum of understanding on the monitor mission to Yugoslavia on the 13th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can you give me the text, madam? What I have here is the Brioni Declaration, Annex II.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I -- there seems to be a problem, Mr. Kostic, with the B/C/S version. Therefore, I think we put the English version on the ELMO. It's -- it's referred to as page 21. Could it please be put on the ELMO, and the section memorandum of understanding - the other side, please - and the lower part. Please move it so we can read the memorandum of understanding, please, so that we can see the lower part. The lower part. Please, the lower part. Yes. It says here that we can see number b). It says here "Article I (Mandate)," and letter b) says here: "To monitor the suspension of the implementation of the declarations of independence for the period of three months, as agreed between the Host Parties, in the context of the arrangements reached in Brioni, particularly on the border regime and the boarder security." Mr. Kostic, in this regard there is no doubt that Brioni included a three-month suspension of the independence declaration; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Brioni Declaration, where three months are mentioned and in the portion that you just read out, it speaks about a three-month period in which the situation at the borders should be returned to what it was, and just on Slovenia. The international borders on Croatian territory were not taken up by the Croatian paramilitaries. It was just the Slovenian paramilitaries that had taken up positions along the borders of Slovenia. And the decision made was to give a three-month deadline - so that's the three months that are mentioned in the Brioni Declaration as well - that in a three-month period a suitable solution be found for the situation along the borders, which would imply solutions which were closely related to those in the European Community. Which means that since it was the military, the JNA, that provided security at our borders and frontiers, that a solution should be found that would imply most probably that police forces should be called upon to protect the borders. So this was the three-month period relating to the frontiers on the territory of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, are you telling us here that the Brioni Declaration and the discussions in Brioni had nothing to do with the suspension of the implementation of the declaration of independence? Are you really telling us that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how do you mean have nothing to do with it? They do have something to do with it, but the Brioni Declaration in no place states that within the space of three months that, unless a solution is found, independence would be proclaimed. The Brioni Declaration speaks about the establishment of peace and that a peaceful settlement should be found to the political crisis, and three months as a suspension period is only mentioned with respect to Slovenia, that the situation should be returned to before the 25th of June where, only when it comes to the question of the border and to protect and secure the border, that would be similar to the European border belt. And there is similarity in the Brioni Declaration and the Presidency decisions taken on 4th of July in fact are none other than attempts for the European Community to fulfil its two obligations taken upon itself as the three points in the package deal when we elected Mr. Mesic as president, which meant suspension of the acts on secession, the establishment of peace, and a political peaceful solution to the problem, along with the simultaneous pressure on the part of the European Community on the Croatian and Slovenian leadership not to block the institutions of the federal state, which means the Presidency, the Assembly, and the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let me just refer to Defence Exhibit D333, tab 68 -- sorry, 86. 86. Mr. Kostic, it is an Assembly of the Republic of Croatia declaration of 8th of October, 1991. This Assembly document refers to the Croatian referendum of the 19 March 1991 -- May 1991. It refers to the date 25 June 1991 that is mentioned in the Brioni Declaration, and it says here: "Having established that the three-month deadline and the deferment of implementation of the constitutional decision determined in the Brioni Declaration expired on 7 October 1991, having established that in the period up to the deadline set in the Brioni Declaration aggressive operations by the so-called JNA and Serbian terrorists against towns and villages gained momentum." Then I drop a few lines, and it says then: "Having established that Yugoslavia no longer exists as an association of states, a joint session of all the Chambers held on 8 October 1991, the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia adopted the following decision: On 8th of October the Republic of Croatia will sever its constitutional ties on the basis of which is created a former SFRY with other republics." And actually, that's the decision taken on the 8th of October, the independence decision. Mr. Kostic, they also refer to the Brioni Declaration. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, your main problem lies in the fact that you wrote the indictment in Zagreb and Zagreb alone, and so many times --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I really reject those kind of comments.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might be allowed to continue my train of thought. As I was saying, so many times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we don't want a train of thought, we just want an answer, a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that thought, another thought. What the lady just read out is what it says in the text, but during my testimony I have shown so many times and with so many examples that the Croatian leadership and Croatian authorities in their attempt and desire to have an independent state interpreted in their own way everything that was mutually agreed upon, including the two truces concluded at The Hague in -- at The Hague conference, which was decided upon with the presence of the top European leaders, and it was an unconditional cease-fire, an unconditional deblocking of the barracks, and they did not do that on either occasion. They interpreted it in their own way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this memorandum of understanding, that document in that group of documents relating to the Brioni Declaration, because our finding is that this memorandum of understanding was not tendered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I'd also like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the number, first?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 946.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would also like to tender this exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I also would like to tender this Defence -- that was originally Defence Exhibit tab 86. Mr. Milosevic, at least as I saw, didn't tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I wonder whether 68 was or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was actually speaking of 86. 68 isn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told I was right. 86 was already admitted. So we'll admit 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will now turn to the 1st of October, 1991. Mr. Kostic, you may remember that in your testimony Judge Bonomy asked to see the official document in which a state of imminent threat of war was declared or concluded, and first of all I would like to show you a clip from an interview that you gave to -- for the documentary "Death of Yugoslavia." And it's in Sanction. And for the AV booth, it's in Sanction. And just before we play that, the transcript should be handed out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] But we needed a two-third majority to pass that decision in the Presidency. Drnovsek did not come to the sessions. Mesic was boycotting them too. Bogicevic and Tupurkovski would come occasionally. It was the session of the 30th of September where the only item on the agenda was the political and security situation in the country. We prepared lengthy conclusions, an eight-page document, which included some provocative stands which we knew would provoke many objections, both by Tupurkovski and Bogicevic, and so on. And towards the end of that document, we sneaked in that formula from -- saying that the country was facing an imminent threat of war. And when we -- the debate started, we spent a lot of time discussing the first part of these -- of the document, these controversial assessments, and then we accepted their objections and removed one sentence from that document and then another, but the assessment that the country was facing an imminent threat of war, the very sentence that exists in the Yugoslav constitution, went unnoticed. They simply did not have any objections to it. And so those conclusions which were carried by two-third majority, by six votes, was published. We gave it to Tanjug. And nobody can deny it happened that way. We have transcript from that session from which you can see that that was the assessment adopted by six votes, that is to say carried by two-third majority. On the next day, Bogicevic and Tupurkovski were reprimanded in writing by Mesic and Drnovsek for attending that session in the first place. And on the next session, Presidency session held on the 3rd of October when we started operating in conditions of an imminent threat of war, they did not appear at all, but that document empowered us to work and make decisions with as many members that were present at the session under the constitution; one, three, or all five members of the Presidency where the peacetime conditions were no longer valid. So we really did use a sort of, if I can say so, political trick, small political trick, but that wasn't the first or the last time such methods were resorted to. But we did this because we wanted to remain within the limits of the constitution defining that question, and we did remain within the limits of the constitution, and we did not take a single law having -- decree law that was not done in that way."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you knew that Mr. Bogicevic and Mr. Tupurkovski would not be in favour of declaring or concluding an imminent threat of war, and that's why you tricked them, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were moments of honesty. I think that that was the case, that it was so, but bear in mind the fact that we were not able to meet one month previously. The country was at war and they boycotted the work of the Presidency. And after their arrival on the 1st of September, Izetbegovic writes a letter to Mesic and Gligorov, criticising why they had attended the Presidency session on the 1st, whereas they took it upon themselves not to block federal institutions. They made that pledge to the international community. So what can I say? I can just confirm what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I was also, as Judge Bonomy, looking for a document where it really actually says that the Presidency concluded or declared that a state of war existed, and actually in all the documents I didn't find that particular official statement. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time when Mr. Bonomy asked that question, at that point I didn't even know that that had been published, for example, in the Official Gazette. Truth to tell, Mr. Bonomy considered and probably still considers that that should have been some sort of separate decision taken. But I am still convinced that it wasn't a decision, it was an assessment of a situation which was the imminent threat of war, and that state of imminent threat of war and that assessment was published in the Official Gazette, and I think that Mr. Milosevic at the following meeting attached this Official Gazette and made it part of the list of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript which we have received, the excerpt from Prosecutor Kostic's interview for television, he said in Serbian, in the Serbian language that -- the following: "That the assessment of an imminent threat of war was placed in the broader text in a fairly unnoticeable manner," whereas in the translation, it says, "We sneaked in that formula," which has quite a different connotation and is not correct. When he says that it wasn't bombastically stated but that it was within the context of the entire text that they used that, that's one thing, but to say "sneaked in that formula" was something rather incorrect. So please bear in mind the fact that the translation, the written translation of what Mr. Kostic really did say in the television interview and this is different, and all that relates to - how shall I put this? - the political tactics does not relate to any sneaking in of anything, but to an unnoticeable way in which this element was introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could we have this clarified, though --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- by placing this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We would have to play it again and it's in the middle of it, or the interpreters could actually --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters agree with the explanation just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, then. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, I would like to tender that clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we thank you for the clarification. And you want to tender --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, this clip. It's an interview given for the documentary "Death of Yugoslavia" but it's not yet tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to have something clarified. What is being tendered, the videotape and not the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you tendering?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are tendering the video clip and the translation as it shows actually on the transcript here in the courtroom. We have the translation and then the clarification of Mr. Milosevic. I think that should actually be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. It's both, of course subject to the clarification has been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, who translated this one? I remember there was -- used to be a general problem of translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The translation was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in relation to "Death of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The translation was made by the people who produced the documentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The BBC.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just help with this, because the translation booth are assisted by getting these documents in advance, and of course will be relying on the documents as the video is playing, and we saw an example there of where Mr. Milosevic made a correction, and of course the interpreter properly accepted that, but of course had been using the document originally provided, which if we -- we must bear that in mind when these problems arise. They are not giving a translation of what is on the video but often with an aided source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The English translation will be marked for identification pending -- pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 947.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I had already moved on to the documents that relate to the 1st of October, 1991. And in relation to Defence Exhibit -- tab 33, that's a statement by the SFRY Presidency of the 1st of October, 1991, I read this document carefully, and I didn't find any official statement that a conclusion was made about an imminent threat of war. It was more or less just, as it appears to me, that there was a talk about a danger of an all-out war breaking out. Can we please have this document in front of everyone. Mr. Kostic, in that document it only says here on the first page in the middle of that page: "The relevant federal departments informed the SFRY Presidency that the political and security situation of the country was extremely serious and dramatic, and that there was danger of an all-out war breaking out." That's actually the information that the Presidency members got. And in the rest of the document I couldn't see anything that -- that it was concluded that such a state of war or imminent threat of a state of war existed. Is that how it went?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text that you referred to is a text of the statement by the Presidency from its session of the 3rd of October. That is the 3rd of October session statement. Now, the 1st of October session, the 1st of October session we were the two-third majority of Presidency members, in conformity with the constitution, took note of the existence and assessed that there was a situation of imminent threat of war. We tried to convene a session for the 2nd - I've already said that - and then at the intervention of Mesic neither Tupurkovski or Bogicevic turned up, so we scheduled it for the 3rd. At their request we moved it forward, but they didn't come then again, and contrary to the constitution, Alija Izetbegovic, as president of the Presidency, made it impossible for Bogicevic to arrive. He did that -- Gligorov did that too, contrary to the constitution, because the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Macedonian Assembly was -- were the only presidencies who could stop them coming to the Assembly session, the FRY Presidency session, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me, this doesn't seem to deal with the point that's arisen. The copy I have of this document is dated the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a mistake, Your Honour. It's actually a mistake in the translation. When you look at the B/C/S, it says the 1st of October. It's mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And therefore it refers to the 30th of September, because it talks about "what happened last night" at the bottom of the page. At the bottom of my page, the last paragraph: "In these circumstances, last night the Supreme Command Staff discussed the possible measures to be taken."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But it is the, as it says here, meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Meeting yesterday. So it's the 30th of September that this relates to on the face of it. I thought it was the 9th of October but now that you've clarified that, it's the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The preceding paragraph has the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Kostic could help us. We have here this document that relates to a Presidency session held "yesterday in Belgrade," and it refers to Bogic Bogicevic, the -- the Assembly session -- sorry, the Presidency session in which Mr. Bogicevic took part in. When did it take place, and does this document that is now in front of you refer to it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. The 1st of October session resulted in a SFRY statement that was broadcast by Tanjug and that we already brought up during the examination-in-chief and tendered into evidence. That is the 1st of October meeting one. And Tanjug, on the 1st of October in the evening, published the Presidency statement, informing the domestic public and the international public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does this document relate to? Can you just clarify that and then we can make some progress.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, this document, which the lady mentioned, and page -- on page 31 of the book is a Presidency statement from its meeting of the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're looking at tab 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please look at tab 33 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Tab 33 is a statement by the SFRY Presidency from a session held on the 1st of October, 1991. It was broadcast by Tanjug on the 1st in the evening. As you can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why -- in that case -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment. In that case, why does it have the date the 1st of October and then start by saying, "The SFRY Presidency held a meeting yesterday in Belgrade"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, this doesn't exist in the original text. It says: "In Belgrade a session of the Presidency of the SFRY was held." It doesn't have the word "yesterday" in the original. You can put the Serbian text on the ELMO and have the interpreters translate it for you. I've been wondering what it was that was in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about the last paragraph, which says: "In these circumstances, last night the Supreme Command Staff discussed" so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "In these circumstances, last night the Supreme Command Staff discussed the possible measures to be taken, and sent a warning to the president of the Republic of Croatia ... and the Main Staff of the Croatian army a warning." It says what they had discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, and in the one, two, three, four, fifth paragraph we have something, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, which comes fairly close to some kind of a formal assessment. The paragraph beginning: "Many lives have been lost," in English. The last sentence reads: "It has been assessed that this poses a serious risk of even fiercer inter-ethnic conflicts and conflicts between the republics and that Yugoslavia was facing an imminent threat of war." So that looks, to me, like an assessment that there was an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this regard, just one question to Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who made this assessment, those who were reporting to the Presidency or the Presidency members themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement adopted by the Presidency of the SFRY in its six-member composition with a two-thirds majority. It was the Presidency of the SFRY that adopted this statement. It considered the situation and concluded that the country was facing an imminent threat of war. All six members of the Presidency adopted this unanimously at a session held on the 1st. During the discussion, what Mr. Milosevic said, that the previous night the Supreme Staff -- the Supreme Command Staff, and so on, was considered and taken into account. This is an assessment of the political and security situation in the country which was adopted just as it stands by all six members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break now. Is there a point you want to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction. Listening to you just a while ago, you quoted the passage mentioning an imminent threat of war. I heard the word "risk." It is not the word "risk" that is used but "threat" in the Serbian text; that there is a threat that all this will happen. "Risk" and "threat" are two different concepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to get into that now. We will take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break I just noticed that the document that we just spoke about, that's Defence Exhibit tab 33 is basically the same document as Exhibit 328, tab 6. However, the translation of tab 33 seems to me more accurate. There are quite some differences in the English translation, therefore my proposal will be to tender this tab 33 so that we have a better version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've already admitted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic -- Mr. Kostic, we have also - and I would like you to have a look at it - we have also some draft minutes from the same Presidency session, and I would like to -- it's tab 328 -- tab 28. It's Exhibit 328, tab 28. That was already used. If you please put the third page with the agenda onto the ELMO -- or, rather, the B/C/S version, please. The B/C/S version with the agenda. Looking at the agenda -- and it's page 3 in the English. Looking at the agenda, it's a quite a lengthy agenda, and there's only the two full points that relate to the situation in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is tab 28, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit 328, tab 28. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where do we get a copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, usually, Your Honour -- I was told usually from exhibits that we have previously tendered, you do not get the copy, but we have put on the ELMO page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I just want to ask you, Mr. Kostic, when you look at the agenda points, there is no mention made of a discussion about an imminent threat of war; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have to be another tab number, because in tab 28 I only have the 17th of August, and that's a single page, both in the Serbian and in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of Prosecution Exhibit 328. It's not in any of the tabs that you have, but it's on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we -- Mr. Usher, could you please move the page so that we can see the -- the end of the page. The lower part. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like you to -- I think, Mr. Kostic, you haven't asked my -- answered my first question. In the agenda there is no mentioning that an imminent threat of war should be discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is the agenda? I see b, c, and d.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we see the English on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 3 there is the agenda, and it continues on page 4. There is just the first two points, where it says: "The political and security situation in the country," and second, "Agreement about further work on finding a solution for the future Yugoslavia," and the rest of the agenda is basically something more or less administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, why is this point, which is a very important one, not on the agenda mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't understand your question, madam. The first item on the agenda is the key item, and it reads: "The political and security situation in the country." Within the scope of this first item on the agenda, the Presidency concluded that the country was facing an imminent threat of war. You don't expect us to discuss this item under Miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now have the B/C/S on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want the B/C/S on the ELMO because the English translation that we have provided within the Exhibit 328, tab 28 is, as we found out now, incorrect, and I would like to clarify this point. On the ELMO, please, the page -- let me see what it is. In the B/C/S it's page 2, and the lower part of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, could you please read the second paragraph under item 1, which starts with "Predsednistvo."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Presidency of the SFRY assessed that the political and security situation in the country is extremely difficult and dramatic and that there is a threat of an all-out civil war." This is what Mr. Mesic wrote in his book when he claimed that an imminent threat of war was not mentioned anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the exhibit that we provided earlier in this case, it actually speaks of "concluded," but as we know now, it is "assessed."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lady said that this is a draft minutes. I see that these are the minutes of the session, judging by the agenda, but as this is a draft, I cannot vouch for the correctness of every single word here. In my book I have the original text of the statement that we issued and which was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's annex 1, page -- and tab 73.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has meanwhile received the shorthand notes of the entire session. We received it in December from the Serbian government or, rather, from Serbia and Montenegro, and it's 136 pages thick document, and we were not able to translate it for this session here. Ms. Tromp, however, has read the entire document, and her finding was that in -- in this document it's not the Presidency members that make assessments but, rather, the institutions, the federal institutions, like Mr. Gracanin and the JNA command. My proposal would actually be that we prepare a complete translation of these shorthand notes and provide it as exhibit from the bar table at the moment when it is actually translated so that everybody can read what is actually said there. That would be my proposal. What we, of course, could do is we could ask Mr. Kostic to go through the B/C/S version and direct us, tomorrow, to the section where the conclusion is made or an assessment is made by the Presidency members and not by anyone else that took part in that session, because in addition to that - because Ms. Tromp provided us with a few bits of translation - and the only page where we actually have mentioning of the state of -- imminent threat of war is on page 26 in the B/C/S, where Mr. Branko Kostic says the following - and maybe you can confirm that, Mr. Kostic - he says: "Firstly, how should we qualify the momentary constitutional legal state in the country? Is it an emergency state, a state of war in the bigger part of the country without the declaration of war, a state of imminent threat of war in the entire country? What is the real influence of the foreign factor onto these happenings? "Secondly, how is the legal and factual subjectivity of Yugoslavia being estimated? In which measures is the SFRY constitution still being respected, and which are the real endurance of the federal organs? How do we provide a minimum functioning in the federation, especially in the domain of defence and security until a solution of the future organisation of the country?" That's questions that Mr. Kostic raised. And do you recall this, Mr. Kostic? And do you recall whether any vote was taken, any conclusion that there was an imminent threat of war by the members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that you have a 136 pages of shorthand notes. Fifteen minute -- 15 years after the event I cannot remember every word you read out. All I can say is that that corresponds to my thoughts at the time. However, I do not know whether this is the original text, these are the original shorthand notes. They always had to be authorised. I don't know if what you are reading from is the authorised version. I can confirm, so that I don't have to read these 136 pages again, in tab 73 on page 339, 340, and 341, and these are just three pages, you have the official statement by the Presidency of the SFRY, which was adopted by all six members of the Presidency. That is a text nobody can dispute. If there are any misunderstandings in this regard, this is the only original text, the only true text that I refer to, that I can vouch for.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you have on the ELMO at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Did you say tab 73 or tab 72, which is your book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the tab number. It's either 72 or 73. It's my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's tab 72. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in my book there is an annex, and that's the original text of the statement. It was published by Tanjug.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in the Prosecution's case, what is the significance of this question of the declaration or conclusion that there was an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
