utterances.text: The position of the Prosecution is that the Presidency -- the six Presidency members did not declare or conclude that there was an imminent threat of war, and therefore that's why the Presidency, the Rump Presidency, as we call it, is illegal, and all the decision and steps they took were illegal. That is the point. In particular, the use of the JNA, and I will come to this point right after I finish this one. The movements of the JNA directed by this Rump Presidency, that's our focus, that this was all illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what you have on the ELMO and what is also marked in the -- for you in the B/C/S is a translation of what you said on page 6 of these shorthand notes, and my question to you was whether the Presidency members ever voted on the conclusion of an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Presidency never voted about the formulation you read out, which purports to be something I said, but they all voted on this statement in which it is concluded that the country is facing an imminent threat of war. This was published, and it was adopted by all six members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, and if I put to you that within this huge document of stenographic notes that we got from the government of Serbia and Montenegro there is no mentioning of any such vote, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that these notes are incomplete, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I now would like to move on to the -- the Presidency session of the 3rd of October, 1991, and it's Exhibit -- it's Prosecution Exhibit 300 -- 328, tab 13. It's draft minutes of the Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we have the -- on the ELMO the B/C/S version. Mr. Usher, the B/C/S version with the first page. It's actually the second page. The second page. Your Honour, I do this exercise because in the translation that we provided to you, we tendered Exhibit 328, tab 13, there is also a translation mistake in there that we find quite important to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, would you read, please, under the -- under the headline "Agenda," there is little paragraph starting with the word "Dogovor." Could you please read this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What passage is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, you have to put the other page. The previous page. The previous page, lower part, please. Further down. Yes. If you read what is standing behind "Dnevni Red."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "1. Agreement on securing continuity of the work of the Presidency of the SFRY, pursuant to the assessment of the Presidency of the SFRY from the 143rd Session of the Presidency of the SFRY of the 1st of October, 1991, on the existence of an imminent threat of war, and passing over to work of the Presidency of the SFRY in conditions of the existence of an imminent threat of war. "2. Some --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to also point out again that it's here "assessment" and not, as it is in the previously provided translation, "conclusion."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, during this session of the Presidency, you actually made quite important changes and decisions, and you say, and I quote now myself from the English - you can now put the English on it, item 1 - "Proceeding from the above assessment --" it's again a change here; assessment -- "the SFRY Presidency noted that the requirements had been met for the SFRY Presidencies to start working and functioning as envisioned by the SFRY constitution in a state of imminent threat of war and in accordance with the SFRY Presidency decision number 36 of the 21st November 1984. The changeover to work in conditions of imminent threat of war will enable the SFRY Presidency to avoid the possibility of having its work --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is kindly asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "... of having its work obstructed and to take over certain functions of the SFRY Assembly, which is unable to convene." And a little bit further down, it says --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation. I'm not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's try again, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I read only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be given to me, the document on the ELMO? I want to see it in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be passed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I start, Mr. Kostic: "The changeover to work in conditions of imminent threat of war will enable the SFRY Presidency to avoid the possibility of having its work obstructed and to take over certain functions of the SFRY Assembly, which is unable to convene." And: "The SFRY Presidency adopted the decision on the work and methods of the Presidency in the event of imminent threat of war which will ensure the continuity of its work. According to the decision, the SFRY Presidency will adopt decisions by a majority vote of its present members." Mr. Kostic, that meant that you could from now on make all the decisions among the four members that attended; right? No more need for six members.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 3rd of October, we could reach decisions with that number of members of the Presidency who were present, based on a simple majority. So if five were present, three votes would be sufficient; if four were present, or three, we could still issue decisions. I wish to draw attention, however, to the following, madam: The document you have quoted from, you yourself stated that these are draft minutes. You see, in the Presidency of the SFRY, there are shorthand or phonographic records. This document becomes valid only after it is authorised by each member of the Presidency. As far as I know, we did not authorise this. Secondly, minutes of the Presidency do not contain any details, only the general gist of the discussion under each item of the agenda. Statements for the public are special documents, separate documents considered at the Presidency and then issued for the public, and one such document is the one I have already mentioned, which is in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, was there any minimum number of members of the Presidency who had to attend to make the meeting valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until the 3rd of October, the Presidency could hold sessions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 3rd of October, pursuant to the decision reached in 1984, if there is an imminent threat of war, there is no minimum number. So the number that can be gathered together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, a little bit further down in that document, it says: "With regards to the implementation of the Decision, it was concluded that all members of the SFRY Presidency be immediately informed that the SFRY Presidency will continue to convene in Belgrade during the imminent threat of war, which makes it necessary for the members of the SFRY Presidency to stay in or near Belgrade, so that the Presidency can begin its work within two hours of convening a session." Mr. Kostic, that does actually exclude Mr. Mesic, Mr. Drnovsek, and the other members that were not close to Belgrade, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not correct on that score, madam. Both Mr. Mesic and Mr. Drnovsek, as well as Mr. Tupurkovski and Mr. Bogicevic, were regularly invited to attend the session of the 3rd of October. They were invited on the 1st of October. We thought that it would be the 1st, then at their request we moved it to the 3rd. They were invited to attend the meeting, and not only that one but every subsequent Presidency meeting that we had, we regularly issued invitations, and Mr. Mesic recognises that in his book. We regularly sent out invitations for the session, with all the attending documents, and Mr. Mesic, 15 days after this, presided over the Presidency meeting in The Hague where we were all present. But they consciously wanted to block the work of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, would it at least be a practical problem for them who are in Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia or Bosnia to come to your sessions? Just from a practical standpoint of view.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it would not present any problem at all, because both Mr. Mesic and Mr. Drnovsek were accommodated in one of those same villas. And in Dedinje they had a 65-square-metre apartment, like I did, and so they lived in those apartments. That was their official accommodation, as it was mine, and it was their duty as Presidency members to live in Belgrade, to reside and work in Belgrade, because it was Belgrade that was the venue of the Presidency sessions. And that also applies to Tupurkovski and Bogicevic, so their place of work was in the Presidency of the SFRY in Belgrade and their accommodation was in Belgrade. Now, the fact that they consciously left Belgrade and Mesic tried to convene and schedule meetings in Brioni or Zagreb or wherever else, the rules governing the Presidency work stipulated that Presidency sessions be held in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the rules also allowed that Presidency sessions could take place at other places, would it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in cases when agreement was reached on the part of all members of the Presidency on that point. But in principle, the Presidency sessions were held in Belgrade. If the Presidency president could assume that a change of venue for the Presidency sessions could not -- might not be accepted by certain members of the Presidency, then he must hold consultations previously, and he cannot schedule a meeting outside Belgrade unless agreement is reached on that point, to change the venue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you said that the other members of the Presidency, as Mr. Mesic and the others, would receive documentations from the Presidency. However, I quote now again from these minutes, and it's still under item 1, it says here: "Also, it was concluded that the members of the SFRY Presidency who were absent from today's session be informed of the contents of this Decision should be informed when they arrive in Belgrade, because it cannot be faxed to them owing to the high degree of confidentiality." Mr. Kostic, I read this to mean that they wouldn't get all the important decisions immediately afterwards but only when they come to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about two quite different matters, madam. I -- what I'm saying is this, that all the Presidency members received material not from the session but material for the session, documents for the session. So they received the documents before the session takes place, not from the session. Now, here they were invited to attend the meeting once the agenda was declared for the 3rd, but they didn't come to the meeting. And then we said that they must be informed, but all the sessions we had after that, for those sessions they received invitations, they received agendas set out in advance, and if they didn't turn up, then we would send back to them the information about what was decided at the sessions in their absence. And Mr. Mesic says that in his book, and he thanks -- expresses thanks to some Mr. Bogicevic and that -- he says that somebody sent him the documents from the offices of the cabinet, but it wasn't that man, it was us. So not from the sessions. Not documents from the sessions but documents for the sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just one more quote from these minutes. It's item 2, the second paragraph. It says: "The SFRY Presidency approved the activities of the Armed Forces Supreme Command so far in implementing the decisions of the SFRY Presidency regarding mobilisation." That's what you did; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there must be a mistake in the text there again, at least as you read it out. You say that that was a draft of some minutes? It wasn't the Supreme Command. We were the Supreme Command. The Presidency was the Supreme Command. And all we could do was to authorise the measures that the staff of the Supreme Command or, rather, the General Staff had taken with respect to mobilisation, and then that is true. With the proviso that Mr. Tudjman had already proclaimed general mobilisation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the original text, it is not state -- it doesn't say "Supreme Command." It says "the work of the staff of the Supreme Command." "The Presidency authorised the work of the staff of the Supreme Command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to Exhibit 328, tab 11, and it's draft minutes of the Presidency session of the 4th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution -- it's a Prosecution exhibit that was provided earlier in the case. That's the Presidency session of the 4th of October. And just under item 1, it says: "The SFRY Presidency adopted the order on partial mobilisation to bring up to strength commands, staffs, units and institutions of the armed forces to ensure their combat readiness." That was done Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That order on partial mobilisation was passed, but not to strengthen the Supreme Command Staff. What it says here quite literally is the following: "The order on partial mobilisation to bring up to strength the commands, the staffs, and units and institutions." So this decision on partial mobilisation was the result of the fact that Slovenia, Croatia, Kosovo, had already taken decisions not to send their recruits to the Yugoslav People's Army, and the Yugoslav People's Army, to all intents and purposes, was cut down in strength under normal conditions whereas war was already going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you don't need to go into details. This was already addressed sufficiently. Under item 2, it says: "The vice-president of the SFRY Presidency briefed the Presidency on the documents related to control and command of the SFRY Armed Forces that he signed in the absence of the president of the SFRY Presidency. In this connection, it was concluded that the vice-president of the SFRY Presidency would continue to sign documents from this domain in the absence of the SFRY president and inform the SFRY Presidency later." First of all, what documents does this first sentence relate to? Which documents did you sign on the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd of October that relate to the military?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the original it doesn't say that they were documents. It -- it says that they were decrees, signed decrees from command. So if we say decree, especially in the field of command of the armed forces, then this refers to acts, to documents that either relate to promotions of certain officers to certain ranks, or possibly it was some sort of recognition and things like that. So those are decrees relating to certain officers, not all of them. And a part of these decrees -- some of these decrees are signed by the minister of defence, some by the chief -- the head of the General Staff, and for the top ranks this is done by the president or vice-president of the Presidency in the absence of the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, my question actually was very precise. I asked you which decrees, or whatever you call it, which decrees you signed in that few days to this briefing on the 4th. What did you sign on the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd of October in relation to the control and command of the SFRY armed forces? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me too much. After 15 years, to tell you what I signed on the 3rd or 2nd of October, what decrees they were, I really can't say. What I did say is that they were decrees either relating to promotion to rank or recognition, commendation, things like that. Those were the sorts of decrees that would be signed. I think I signed decrees about new officers having completed the military academy and the new commissioned officers. But of course you can get more information about that from the people that sent you this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And would they also have, Mr. Kostic, the final version of these minutes confirmed by all members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean these minutes here, this record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You made the point that these are drafts, that the minutes are draft minutes and that they are ultimately confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we didn't confirm the minutes. Truth to tell, minutes were adopted. So minutes from the previous session would be adopted at the forthcoming session. The minutes as minutes just states roughly what the items on the agenda were. However, the stenographic notes from each Presidency session, especially if they go public, have to be authorised beforehand. So every participant in the discussion at Presidency sessions, if these are going to be made public, has to authorise - I don't know what the deadline is, within the space of three days or five days - and only once it has been authorised can the shorthand notes of meetings of that kind go public, whereas the minutes are adopted from one session to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. So wherever you have a draft, there is a subsequent authorised version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be one. But as I say, an authorised version of the stenographic notes, where every word of participants in the session is recorded. Not an authorisation of the overall minutes compiled by the Secretary-General of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you said that the other members of the Presidency that were not coming any more, they did that because they didn't want to come. This is at least my understanding. They had opportunity to come. And I would like to play now an intercept to you. For the AV booth, it's on Sanction. And it is Exhibit 613, tab 123. It is an intercept between Radovan Karadzic and Mr. Kostic, held on the 18th of November, 1991, and it's quite a lengthy intercept, and we only play a little sequence of it where it relates to the work of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Yes, yes, we took this man Bogicevic to talk to him and see what we're going to do. "That he should do his job for which he took the solemn oath. He doesn't have to vote in favour, he can vote against. "Well, I'm not sure either. He wants the constitutional basis, we'll give him -- we discussed the Prime Minister. "Yes. "You know that some people mentioned me there. "Slobo told me -- well, it wouldn't be a good idea. I have to finish what I started here. That's the most important thing. And on the other hand, we need a technician, somebody who knows how to manage the system. I sent Jovic a fax, a message that the Serbian Democratic Party does not have its candidate or a Bosnian candidate, and we considered that Serbia that had not -- did not have a Prime Minister for 30 years, that it should be Serbia who should provide -- which should provide a Prime Minister."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise for not having the written text of the tape played.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, first of all in relation to this conversation, it's you and Mr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that is certainly Radovan Karadzic's voice. As to my voice, as you were able to mention, is very indistinct. Quite possibly -- I often listened to tapes of my conversations and public appearances, and I must say it is very difficult for me to recognise my own voice very often, so I really can't confirm whether, from what you've just played, from the intercept you've just played, whether the other person on the line was me, whether that was my voice or not. But what I can say is this: On the basis of the contents of the conversation, I don't exclude the possibility that it is my voice as well. And if it's me and Mr. Radovan Karadzic talking at a certain point when we as the Presidency tabled to the federal parliament an expose, and when the Federal Executive Council of the Assembly withdrew its trust from Mr. Ante Markovic, and when Ante Markovic was revoked and a new Prime Minister about to be nominated, we addressed all the republics that in keeping with procedure they should put forward their own candidates for president of the federal government. So that's what I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Kostic, you are discussing here with Mr. Karadzic about the role of Bogicevic. To me it sounded as if you didn't want him to participate in the Presidency, or that there was at least a problem with him participating in the Presidency. Is that my misunderstanding or what does -- what was that about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, quite obviously you've misunderstood. All I could have done was to complain to Radovan Karadzic and say that Mr. Bogicevic was obstructing the work of the Presidency. And as you were able to see from his response, he says that they talked to him, too, and were trying to indicate the constitutional foundations. And the Bosnian constitution is quite clear on this point, and I'll tell you that later on, where it is only the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina that can revoke Bogicevic's participation in the work of the Presidency. I was complaining that Mr. Bogicevic, like the others, was obstructing the Presidency and trying to block its work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now move on to another topic, and I would like to have Exhibit 338, tab 2 in front of the witness. It's an exhibit previously tendered by the Prosecution. It's an order of the 1st of October, 1991, signed by Mr. Bulatovic in his function as president of the Presidency of Montenegro, and it says here under "Order": "On 2 October 1991, between 1500 and 1700 hours, carry out a mobilisation of a Special Police Unit the strength of a reinforced Infantry Company tasked with carrying out combat operations of the armed forces in the conflict of war on the border of Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia." And it says as item II: "Together with units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, the unit will perform specific military and police tasks in accordance with the Mission Plan to be devised by the Operative Command on the Dubrovnik front." Mr. Kostic, it's on -- this order is of the 1 October 1991, and on that same day the Rump Presidency or, as you like it, reduced Presidency starts to function. That's not a coincidence; right? That's related.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. You see that this order of Mr. Momir Bulatovic is entitled the 1st of October, and the Presidency in its reduced form started working only on the 3rd of October. On the 1st of October we had six members working. So that conclusion is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This order, does that relate to an extensive military campaign in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this order. And you could ask Mr. Bulatovic about that. This is the involvement of a police unit, engagement of a police unit numbering about one company strong. All I know is that at the time in Montenegro, the initiative was launched and that Montenegro at the time there was a reinforced police unit that was sent to the border between Montenegro and Croatia, and in that border belt, because for 20 years when we didn't have a single armed soldier over there, much more numerous Croatian police forces appeared in the area, and paramilitaries as well, that started to threaten the border and our barracks, the JNA barks at Prevlaka. Otherwise, Mr. Bulatovic, pursuant to the constitution, as president of the Yugoslav State Presidency, was placed -- the person best placed to take a decision of this kind. But this decision of Mr. Bulatovic has nothing to do with the Presidency moving to working within conditions of an imminent threat of war, because this was on the 1st of October and it was only on the 3rd that we began working in reduced composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know about this mobilisation of police forces in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, no. I learnt about that later on. It didn't come within my purview so it wasn't my duty to know things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the Rump Presidency took over, the -- the JNA --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, can we use the other term, the "reduced Presidency" as a term instead of the "rump"? I think that Mr. Robinson gave the right term. Unless you want to implement Mr. Mesic's terminology to the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... issue an edict on this. I leave it to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I use this term because it's used in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I just tell you I will use it because it's used in the indictment and therefore I stick to it, but you, of course, can call it whatever you like. Mr. Kostic, at that time when the Rump Presidency took over, that was a few days before the moratorium on the suspension of the independence of Croatia and Slovenia came up, the deadline came up. Does that -- did you make all this decision because of that? Is that related?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had nothing to do one with the other, because we were surprised by the decision of the 8th of October, and I said that the 8th of October decision cannot find support in the Brioni Declaration anyway, it can only find a point of support in the one-sided interpretation by the Croatian leadership of the contents of the Brioni Declaration. So that we really didn't expect that anything special would happen on the 8th of October, anything --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, also on the 1st of October -- no. Rather, let us play first an intercept. There is another intercept which I would like you to listen to, and it's Exhibit 613, tab 128, and it's an intercept again between you and Mr. Karadzic. At the time it's on the 26th of November, 1991, and again it's on Sanction and we play it because it's not long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Hello? "Good morning. "Hello, Radovan, how are you? "How are you? "I'm fine. I was on another telephone yesterday, but I wanted to see how we could suggest this about Ploce."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have the transcript of the intercept, and the sound isn't clear enough for us to follow without it being placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Please, can you put it on the ELMO, Usher, so that they can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Hello? "Hello. "Hi, Radovan. "How are you? "Fine, how are you? "Excellent. Listen, I was on Nikola's phone yesterday, so I don't know what the situation is like, and I thought we could discuss how we could suggest this communication from Ploce, because Ploce is vital to us. "Yes. "And they can take the part from Ploce downward. "Towards Dubrovnik? "Yes. "Uh-huh. "Is there any chance of that happening? "Well, I don't know. We agreed that they would come with detailed maps, you know. "Uh-huh. Maybe they should be told that somebody in Bosnia believes, that, for example, our side believes that Ploce is of great importance and that it has destroyed the Bosnian economy so far, and that it should -- maybe it would be a good thing to do, it seems to me, since Yugoslavia can -- Requests regarding that have already been made. "... the Neretva, right? "A bit to the left of the Neretva. "A bit to the left of the Neretva. "Yes, a few kilometres, a bit. "All right, I'll bear that in mind. We'll see, then we'll also see about that with those people from the army. "Yes, well, that is the Bosnian economy, but it should, yes, no, it won't be able to oppose. On the contrary. "Yes. "Because everything depends on down there, entirely. "Okay. "And inside, on the mainland - nothing, we must not consider it. One side is entirely against it and there's nothing there in the end, and the army can have full control over it. "All right. The Neretva, practically that is-- defend it with the idea of demilitarisation of Dubrovnik, like the surrounding area. "Yes, and the surrounding area, and Plo ... "Practically, to demilitarise that whole pocket. "Yes, all of it, and Ploce are a strategic importance there and generally they are of economic importance. So it can be said that ... it can be requested that Ploce should be -- "Okay, I'll take that into account. "Good. "So there while we're discussing it, for the army, a bit about that. "Okay. I think that would be a good idea. "Okay. "They have the means to defend themselves. "Okay. "All right, speak to you later."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you are speaking here with Mr. Karadzic on quite massive operations of the JNA, right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. It wasn't a large-scale operation at all. The units of the JNA at the time were already on the territory of Dubrovnik. I already said that I was not clear myself why the Supreme Command Staff sent 30.000 to such a small area. And the assignment of those units was not to take over Dubrovnik, and on one occasion I just presented my assumptions, that I don't exclude the possibility of the General Staff or, rather, the staff of the Supreme Command at that time having requested the Supreme Command to have mobilisation of up to 150.000 men and that the Yugoslav People's Army should then cut across certain axes on Croatian territory and reach the barracks where our 25.000 army members were located, to disarm the Croatian paramilitaries, and then to bring Tudjman to the negotiating table, because all negotiations had proved unsuccessful to date. So that I don't exclude the possibility that it was precisely the General Staff by sending out such large numbers, such large units to such small territory perhaps had the intention of reaching the Neretva River and joining up with the Knin Corps up there, and so on and so forth. But it wasn't any separate massive operation that we were planning. Here Mr. Karadzic in this conversation just leads us to the conclusion, because there was a lot talked about the need to demilitarise the entire area of Dubrovnik and the surrounding parts. So we considered that this demilitarisation of the Dubrovnik belt could be a good solution and linked to the problem of the Prevlaka as well, which shuts off the entrance to the Bay of Kotor. So within the frameworks of all those negotiations, discussions, and talks, Mr. Karadzic is talking about the port of Ploce which was treated as a Bosnian and Herzegovinian port in peacetime, and he highlights that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you said you cannot exclude the possibility that there was such bigger operation goals in existence, but you are actually talking with Mr. Karadzic about that, and for this purpose I would like to use the atlas again. That's Exhibit 336, page 37 and 36. Mr. Kostic, you are speaking about Ploce, and we find Ploce at the coast in quarter 2 -- 1, 3, and you speak about Ploce, which is in the Neretva Delta, and we see -- we hear you speak about the Neretva River. That's not just Dubrovnik, that's about a huge territory; right? Ploce is a little bit upwards, south-west -- north-west. North-west, yes. Ploce. And then you have the Neretva River between Mostar and the coast. So this is actually what you are also talking about. And my question to this is: At that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness hasn't found the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No? I think he pointed at Ploce.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Neretva River. My question to you is: At that time, the Bosnian Serbs had actually six goals, strategic objectives. Do you know about these strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the six strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian leadership, I really don't know about these. I can find Ploce and Neum here. I knew and had known previously that Ploce was practically the main port of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even for part of Croatia, because they used communications going through Bosnia. Bosnia had a small part of the coast at Neum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in that territory between Ploce and Dubrovnik, there were no barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So there was no reason to attack this area; right? Other than what you already mentioned that link up certain corps and certain territories.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, madam, the JNA never attacked that area at all. I assert that with confidence. The JNA did not go any further than Slano. I didn't visit this part of the coast many times, so I'm not really sure of the distance. But as far as I know, the JNA didn't even get as far as Neum. It was at Cepikuce, Slano, but it didn't go further up. You should know that at that time the Serbian leadership of Bosnia and the leadership of the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia were having intensive talks at the time about Bosnia getting certain territory around the port of Ploce, and so on and so forth, should Croatia secede. They were discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kostic, in that territory that you just mentioned where the JNA was actually heavily involved, there were -- there was no Serb majority and not even a substantial minority of Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said, madam, that the JNA went there to protect the Serb ethnic majority. The JNA went there to block Dubrovnik and the surrounding area and thereby prevent the spreading of the flames of war to the territory of Montenegro. Also, to protect the barracks on the peninsula of Prevlaka. Just as the army did not set out to conquer Dubrovnik, it only set up a military blockade, a naval blockade there in order to prevent the war spreading to Montenegro. That was the main task of the JNA in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you said that at that time the leadership, the Serbian leadership and the leadership of Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia were having talks on Ploce. Who exactly did have these talks, and could it be that you confused this with talks in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who had discussions at the time, but I know that for the Serb people in Bosnia who were expecting some sort of independence within the framework of Bosnia, the issue of Ploce as a port and of railroads and transport was very, very important when one could sense that Croatia was about to be recognised and become independent. These talks were more between Bosnia and Croatia than inter-ethnically within Bosnia, but I really don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, before we move on to other questions about the JNA, just one further remark in relation to the session of the Presidency held on the 1st of October, 1991. I asked you whether the actions in relation to the -- the changes of the Presidency on the 1st of October and the following one, I asked you whether it had anything to do with the expiring of the deadlines for Croatia and Slovenia, and you said it didn't. However, I have -- I quote now from these extensive stenographic notes, and on page 44 in the B/C/S, and here is the translation: Mr. Milivoje Maksic says: "They agreed on the following: In a still to be prepared declaration, all sides in Yugoslavia will, after the expiration of the moratorium, be called upon to continue the participation in the Conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague ..." and so on and so forth. It was discussed, Mr. Kostic, on that 1st of October, and you were aware that this was upcoming, and it played a role, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can draw your own conclusions, madam, but what you have just quoted is the opinion of Milivoje Maksic. He was the deputy of Mr. Loncar, the federal secretary for foreign affairs. I really don't remember this, but even if I did, such a statement by Mr. Maksic would only go to confirm our expectations that a peaceful political solution would be found rather than a solution based on violence and force. We hoped it would be found at The Hague conference. Six days after -- or, rather, 23 days earlier, on the 7th of September, at a session of the Presidency we agreed on the four basic principles which Mr. Mesic set out at the first inaugural conference in The Hague. These principles were agreed on by all the members of the Presidency and all the republican presidents. I don't actually remember what Mr. Maksic said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when discussing Defence Exhibit D333, tab 67, that was the 7th May 1991 declaration of the top command of the JNA in raising combat readiness, you said that throughout all of 1991 and 1992 the JNA acted with restraint.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that's on transcript page 47732.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept saying, and I still assert today that throughout the war crisis in the former Yugoslavia the JNA acted with extreme restraint. No other army would have acted with such restraint. The JNA suffered enormous losses, respected all cease-fires, was always under threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We don't need to repeat that. I just asked you and you confirmed that you said that. However, I have here a Tanjug report on a declaration, a statement of the Supreme Command headquarters of the SFRY armed forces of 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it was part of the Exhibit 643, tab 1 or, rather, it's mentioned in the report of the military expert Mr. Theunens. It was not tendered separately. It's just mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to quote from what is said here. And as you say, Tanjug is usually correct in its reporting. And in the lower part of the document, it says: "For each attacked and overrun of Yugoslav People's Army facility, one facility of vital importance of the Republic of Croatia will be immediately destroyed. "2. For each attack and taken garrison, vital facilities of the town in which the garrison is located will be destroyed. The civilian population is warned to withdraw in time from inhabited places. "3. As a military response to taking several barracks and other military facilities since the latest cease-fire agreement, we will launch offensive actions in part of the Republic of Croatia." Mr. Kostic, that's on the 1st of October. That's quite now different from being a buffer between ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this was after ten cease-fires had been agreed, and in each of these it was the obligation of the Croatian paramilitary formations to lift the siege of the JNA barracks. Great Britain moved its whole armada to the Falklands, and our members on their own territory were under threat from the unconstitutionally established paramilitary formations of Croatia which we had tolerated for months. I know about this warning issued by the Supreme Command Staff, and it only goes to confirm what I said. They were fed up. They were fed up waiting for the Croatian paramilitaries to respect the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we're going to take the break now. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in that warning that was made by the Supreme Command headquarters, there is no more a distinction made between civilian and military targets. You know that targeting civilians and civilian institutions and facilities could be a war crime; right? You know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could represent a war crime, yes, but if vital facilities are being targeted which can be used by the paramilitaries to make it impossible to bring water, electric power, telephone communications, and similar things, then of course the army can threaten to destroy such facilities. And as you may have seen, the army issued warnings to the civilian population, telling them to take refuge in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when you heard and got aware of this warning, what did you do about it? Did you address the Supreme Command Staff about it and warn them that what they are threatening here could be -- amount to war crimes? Did you do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you I read and learned about this warning when preparing for this testimony. At the time, I was not aware of this warning, but I reiterate: If the Croatian paramilitaries were counter-constitutionally cutting off water, electricity, telephone communications --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We need to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't necessarily understand those three paragraphs in that way. Why shouldn't it be assumed that they're talking about military facilities?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What he is actually -- what is actually stated here in paragraph 1 -- in point 1, it's actually that they want to destroy a facility of vital importance for Croatia, and there is no distinction between whether it's military or civilian. And in one -- in the next one it's even more clear, at least to me. It says here, "Vital facilities of the town." That, to me, actually can or will include civilian facilities. At least, there is no distinction made. And it is said here: "The civilian population is warned to withdraw in time from inhabited places." In other words, they want to -- to retaliate on inhabited places. That's why I actually put this to Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. I think there may be some basis for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You cannot -- you could not locate the document other than the -- Mr. Theunens' report yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We actually have only this -- this previous translation. That's a translation made on the basis of this original Tanjug domestic service report, and we don't have the report as such. However, I would like to tender this document, Your Honour, as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have the B/C/S version as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, we don't. That is what we don't have, Your Honour. We just have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we heard from the witness that he confirmed the authenticity or the content of this document? He just dealt with it. Could you confirm it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, Mr. Theunens dealt with it, and Mr. Theunens referred to this item in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this was not admitted at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. It was just -- there were so many exhibits related to Mr. Theunens' report that only part of it were tendered officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Professor Kostic, you do not dispute the existence of this order or report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I looked at the English version of this. I cannot say this is the very document, but I do know that in the collection of documents I have in which one can find all the decisions and orders issued by the Presidency of the SFRY and the Supreme Command Staff, I think I saw a similar document in the Serbo-Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this must come from somewhere originating in the B/C/S language, and that's really what this Court should be given primarily. I think this document should be marked for identification pending production of an original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do as Mr. Kay has suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just in this context, you said that there -- you -- you have read something in a collection of documents. What kind of collection would it be, and do you have it? Could you provide the B/C/S to us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it with me at present, but I can bring it tomorrow morning, if I can find it. I don't have it here now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That would be very helpful, if you could do that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 948, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like also, Your Honour, as we are dealing with exhibits, I would like to tender the -- the stenographic notes of the -- of the Presidency session of 1 October, as far as I have quoted them, and it's the quote related to page 26, Branko Kostic. And the other one is related to page 44, Milivoje Maksic's remark. And as I said before, I would like to, from the bar table, if we have completed the entire translation, we would want to submit it from the bar table. It will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is inquiring whether the witness confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I understood him to confirm this, that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit those pages to which reference was made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 949.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would now like you to look at another statement made by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, and it's Exhibit 446, tab 64, and perhaps we have the first page -- first page of this document on the ELMO. It's a document dated 12 October 1991, of the Administration for Moral Guidance within the SSNO. And I just quote from the bottom of this document. It says here: "It is obvious that the war which has been imposed upon the Serbian people in Croatia and the JNA by the Ustasha forces and their leadership, is not about the conquest of Croatian territory, as some peacemakers falsely insinuate and pretend. It is rather about defending parts of the Serbian people from genocide and biological extermination with which they are threatened by resurrected fascism in Croatia, securing the safe withdrawal of the JNA forces currently under blockade and families ..." and so forth. Mr. Kostic, the JNA is not a buffer here according to their own statement. They are now defending parts of the Serbian people; right? And that's October.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have repeated several times: Initially in April, May, and even in June 1991, the JNA was really acting as a buffer, separating the conflicting sides and preventing the spread of inter-ethnic conflicts. However, as the Croatian paramilitary formations grew in size, and I did mention that in only two months the number of policemen was increased from 17.000 to 90.000 men, as they grew in size and numbers and armed themselves, they intensified their attacks on the JNA. I have stated more than once during this testimony that one of the strategic aims of the JNA was to ensure the physical protection of the imperiled Croatian -- of the imperiled Serbian people --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- where they were in the majority. When the United Nations sent in the Blue Helmets with the priority task of defending the Serbian population, the JNA withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, there is also on the next page, page 2 in the English and I think also in the Serbian, it says: "That is why the SFRY Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has taken a clear position that the JNA units withdrawal from Croatian territories inhabited by Serbs would be unacceptable because that would expose them to physical liquidation ..." and so on and so forth. Mr. Kostic, those units, the JNA units within that territory inhabited by Serbs, their barracks were not at that time blockaded, right? The blockaded barricades were in other parts of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks located on the territories where there was a majority Serbian population were not blockaded. It was the barracks on the territory of Croatia which had been there in peacetime, where there was a majority Croatian population, that were blockaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And one last quote from this document here. It's the very last paragraph. It says here in the first line: "All armed units, be they JNA, Territorial Defence, or volunteer units must act under the single command of the JNA." That's what you have already also mentioned that did happen; right? The JNA were in command of all the troops.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question was that indeed this did happen. The JNA on the ground were in command of all these troops that are listed here in that paragraph that I just read; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on national defence, all armed units were under the command of the JNA. This includes the police force, the Territorial Defence, and the regular units of the JNA. They all had to act in unison. However, we were unable, when some paramilitary units were formed by some opposition parties, to put these under the control of the JNA. The task of the JNA was, however, to prevent those units from operating on that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about Arkan's unit, Arkan's Tigers? Were they also included under the JNA command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. I couldn't say that. I don't know if and when Arkan's units were there. The only thing I know for certain is that in Western Slavonia, the volunteers sent by Mr. Seselj's Serb Radical Party did not go there as separate volunteer units of Mr. Seselj's but, rather, they joined the JNA and Territorial Defence units. As for Arkan's men, I really don't know if, when, or where they were put under the control of the JNA. I don't know if they were under their control or not. And the same goes for the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, during your testimony on Monday, at transcript 48056 and 48557, you referred to the composition of the JNA, and you said that even in 1992 in both the General Staff and in many units there were non-Serbs from the highest to the lowest level. When you said that, Mr. Kostic, the Office of the Prosecutor actually looked at the commanders of corps and military districts that relates to Croatia, and I would like to put some names to you to see whether this was correct what you told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have here a sheet with all these names. I think just for ease of reference, it's better that everybody has it in front of everyone. It's easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we do not need to speak about Mr. Kadijevic, Brovet, and Adzic because we have already mentioned them quite frequently. Also, Zivota Panic, we have spoken about him as well. General -- Major General Mile Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How far down do you go for the seniority?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I go down to the commanders of the operational groups and tactical groups. Not below that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the first one I just want to mention here, Mile Mrksic, major general, commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade. He's a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We don't need --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't expect too much of me, that kind of data, because of these officers on the list here, I know very few of them except those who were at the top of the General Staff with whom I communicated. So I won't be able to give you reliable data as to the ethnicity of all these people there, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I thought you as the member of the Presidency and Supreme Command would know at least the generals. But let's see how it goes. It says here Aleksandar Spirkovski. He was commander of the 1st Military District. He --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He was replaced in September 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he was replaced, but I do know that he's a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Zivota Panic, his successor actually, he is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Vojislav Djurdjevac, from the 4th Corps, command of the 4th Corps Sarajevo, what is he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Commander of the 5th Corps, Nikola Uzelac, is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Vladimir Vukovic, commander of the 5th Corps after Uzelac, is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think that he would be a Montenegrin rather than a Serb, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Momir Talic, commander of the 5th Corps, Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mladen Bratic, commander of the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you don't know these people, just look down the list and tell me whether you can identify any of them being a non-Serb and non-Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is Konrad Kolsek, for example, is a Slovene, and I knew him personally because he was corps commander in Podgorica a long time before that. He's a Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And he was replaced in July 1991 by Zivota -- Zivota Avramovic. Is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The one replacing --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is he, a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The one replacing Mr. Kolsek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is a Serb, but I really can't say, this national composition. I see Vladimir Vukovic appears twice here. I don't know if it's the same man or not. Ratko Mladic is a Serb. Miodrag Jokic is a Montenegrin. Zvonko Jurjevic is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he was replaced --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Anton Tus, for example, was a Croat. He was the commander of the air force. Anton Tus escaped to a paramilitary organisation of Tudjman's --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and instead of him, there was Jurjevic Zvonko who was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you do not answer my question. I was asking you whether Mr. Zvonko Jurjevic, the Croat, was replaced by Bozidar Stevanovic, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, Zvonko Jurjevic was replaced, but it is very important in view of the substance of your question for me to answer this. Zvonko Jurjevic was appointed commander of the air force instead of Anton Tus who was himself a Croat who had fled to join up with Tudjman's paramilitary to all intents and purposes, and we had nothing against appointing another Croat as commander of the air force. Now, he was replaced, the second commander was replaced, whether intentionally or not. The UN helicopter on a mission was shot down. I think there was some Italians and some Frenchmen there, and we thought this was a direct mistake on the part of the commander of the air force, and that's why he was replaced, because we thought that the downing of that UN helicopter, they wished to undermine our actions and drive to bring in the UN peace forces to Bosnia. I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we don't need all these details. It was a simple question. And I understand Mr. Bozidar Stevanovic is indeed a Serb. Now, we look at the 2nd Military District of Sarajevo. You know Milutin Kukanjac. He was a Serb; right? And Mr. Ratko Mladic definitely too; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the Operational Group commanders, we have here Andrija Biorcevic of the Operational Group North, involving Baranja and for northern part of Eastern Slavonia, he was a Serb or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for certain. All I can do about these other people -- Spiro Nikovic is a Montenegrin, Pavle Strugar is a Montenegrin. As to the other people on that second page, I really don't know. Judging by the name, name and surname, I can assume they might be Serbs but I don't know their ethnicity because I don't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And besides those listed, can you name any high-ranking - I mean really high-ranking - non-Serbian officer who was still in command in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you that most of these generals here are one -- people I don't know. I never met them, never saw them. The ones I do know is Kadijevic, Brovet, Adzic, Panic. As to the others, I don't know them. You could have asked Mr. Vasiljevic that, who was a witness of yours. He could have given you all that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let's move on. I would like to now refer you again to the testimony of Mr. Jovic, and actually paragraph 84 of his 89(F) statement. Your Honour, that's Exhibit 596, tab 1. Mr. Kostic, Mr. Jovic refers here to a meeting before the Presidency session on 11 July 1991, and he says -- he says here the following: "On 11 July 1991, before the Presidency session, Kadijevic, Milosevic, Kostic and I met. We assessed that the JNA cannot remain united." I skip now a few lines, and then it says --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be given the document in Serbian, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have it at hand, Your Honours. You have to listen to the translation, Mr. Kostic, but it's only very brief sections. And it says here: "Internal orientation, defending the future Yugoslavia. First variant of defending the future Yugoslavia: Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs outside Serbia and possibly Macedonia. Second variant: Serbia, Montenegro, the Serb nation in Yugoslavia, and possibly something else." Do you recall having this meeting where you discussed the future Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't remember that, that Mr. Jovic refers to in his book. We did have very frequent consultations, almost on a daily basis. Now specifically what he says here, I really don't remember any of that. He claims again -- or ten days later, if you say it was on the 4th of July. I think on the 14th of July we took the decision to withdraw police forces from Slovenia. This was on the 18th. He put this in order in the form of a diary but quite obviously he did not keep a diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He actually speaks of a meeting of 11 July 1991, but we don't need to dwell on the date. Mr. Kostic, the first variant, as it is called here, of the future Yugoslavia, including Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs outside Serbia, and possibly Macedonia, is that basically reflecting the Belgrade Initiative that you have already spoken about or is it different?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Jovic's thoughts on that were during those days and how he wrote it down, but what we were thinking about and the what -- the way my thoughts were going has been repeated many times and written down many times. We considered that quite obviously Slovenia -- we cannot keep Slovenia and Croatia within the composition of Yugoslavia. I personally considered, and all the other people that I associated with said that we should not use the force of the Yugoslav People's Army to force anybody to live together. And I must say that to the last day, practically, we did think that that reduced Yugoslavia would include Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republic in its entirety with Montenegro and Macedonia. And as for the Serb people who were under threat on the territory of Croatia, where they were an ethnic majority, we had a very clear-cut vision that that people over there must be physically protected with the Yugoslav People's Army until a political settlement had been found or, rather, until the Blue Helmets had arrived who would take on the role of physical protector, and then we withdrew the Yugoslav People's Army from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the second variant that you -- that you were discussing, according at least to Mr. Jovic, that's including Serbia, Montenegro, and the Serb nation in Yugoslavia and possibly somewhere else, that's actually the same that was later the territories that you discussed in -- on the Convention on Yugoslavia on the 3rd of January, 1992; right? That's basically the same, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I cannot tell you what went on in Mr. Jovic's head. He was a witness of yours, and you could have asked him yourself about matters of that kind. All I can do is to confirm what was quite clear to me and my own personal options dating back to those days, is that on the one hand we had no pretensions towards Serb territories in Croatia, and the best proof of that is that the UN peace forces were invited over by us. We had no pretensions, secondly, towards Bosnia, and it is clear from day one we supported both the Cutileiro Plan and the Vance-Owen Plan, without excluding the possibility that in some -- at some point in future there should be a redeployment of those forces in the Balkans which would lead to some sort of unification, but we rejected as the Yugoslav state Presidency, and the Assembly of Yugoslavia rejected --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let me interrupt you. I had actually -- I thought I had asked a very simple question. Were the two -- were two concepts discussed on a future Yugoslavia? One with Bosnia and one without.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, what do you expect me to say? You want to hear what you want to hear? I said that I don't specifically remember that particular meeting, but I also said how I thought and what my thoughts were and all those making decisions and all the people that had the greatest responsibility was what I described a moment ago. We even rejected including the Serbs within Yugoslavia and nominating the representative to the Presidency of the SFRY. So you can't expect me to say what you want to hear. I'm telling you what our thoughts were, and I can confirm that with steps taken, with documents written, with -- and so on, the way we thought at that time. Now, what Mr. Jovic thinks and what his calculations were, well he was a witness of yours here and you can call him back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I will go on and now I will quote from paragraph 86 of the 89(F) statement of Mr. Jovic. It's related to a meeting of the 8th of August, 1991, and he says here: "... Milosevic, Kostic, Kadijevic, Adzic and I met to agree on the further political orientation in connection with the decision on the cease-fire in Croatia. Milosevic insisted on heightening combat readiness by the military because he felt that further clashes were imminent. He asked, almost insistently, when and where the military would finally begin the definitive showdown ..." And also as the second last sentence mentioned: "We really have no alternative but to intensively expel the Croats and Slovenes from the military ..." Do you recall such a meeting and such a conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither recall such a meeting nor such a conversation. In my testimony and in my book when I never -- when it never entered my mind that I would appear here before The Hague Tribunal or be mentioned as a party to the joint criminal enterprise or as a witness in this trial, I stated quite clearly there and wrote down that Mr. Milosevic was precisely one of those people who, when we had to decide whether to undertake an offensive action through the force of the army to deblock the barracks in Croatia, was the man who did not accept that solution. And I have to say that in my intimate thoughts I considered that my ideas were more proper. And I also said that, although I didn't comment this with him, he didn't accept to take steps like that because it would have involved far more widespread mobilisation. So perhaps he was afraid that mobilisation would not have succeeded in Serbia, and an unsuccessful mobilisation in Serbia with the Socialist Party in rule could threaten that and could lead to civil war. I wrote that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, again, I'm now referring to paragraph 91 of -- 91 of the Jovic 89(F) statement, and he speaks here about the meeting on the 24th September 1991, including again you, Kadijevic, Milosevic, and Mr. Jovic, and he says here, it's at the end of this chapter: "Kadijevic then concluded the following: Military success cannot be achieved with a semi-legitimate Yugoslavia. Serbia and Montenegro should declare that the military is theirs and assume command, financing the war, and everything else. All the generals on the General Staff, except one, are Serbs, and they all support this approach and think the same way. We could not accept, says Jovic -- We could not accept the demand that the military drop 'Jugoslav' from its name. That would mean Serbia and Montenegro would completely lose all their advantages, both politically and military ..." And just to add to this, in paragraph 94, he says: "At the meeting of the 6th -" and it's now two days -- "on the 28th of September, Kadijevic again raised the question of the state for whom the army should fight for, and last time he offered to run the JNA over to Serbia and Montenegro. And since Serbia and Montenegro do not have their own armies, a formula should be found for turning the JNA over to those nations that want to remain in Yugoslavia. However, this was felt to be bad solution from the international standpoint." Mr. Kostic, do you recall that Mr. Kadijevic raised such issues and that they were rejected by the other members in these meetings because of international reasons or advantages?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that conversation. As I say, we had many. Mr. Jovic is writing about that in his diary. Mr. Jovic also wrote down that he came to see me. He never came to see me. Now, what his intentions were, I don't know. He claims that Mr. Milosevic sort of seemed a bit disoriented. I must say that I had a lot of communication with Mr. Milosevic, and that I never found him to be confused. I think he was much broader in his outlook than Mr. Jovic at that point in time. Now, why Mr. Jovic wrote these things and that he has turned it into a diary as having been recorded in his notebook as a diary, you'll have to take that up with him. But at no point were my thoughts along those lines, nor Mr. Bulatovic's, although he is not mentioned here, nor Mr. Milosevic's thoughts, and the thoughts of the top military echelons to establish a Serbian and Montenegrin army. Instead, we always started out from the fact that it was the Yugoslav People's Army. He always mentioned the date of the 28th of September. Don't forget that that was at that time still the sole legitimate state member of the United Nations, no question of recognising Croatia or Slovenia or their independence or anything like that. So thoughts along those lines can only be the result of Mr. Jovic's line of thinking and not my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I didn't ask you about Mr. Jovic. I simply asked you whether the military at that time made such demands. It's Mr. Kadijevic, at least according to Mr. Jovic, making such demands which are then rejected by the politicians in the group of six. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember Mr. Kadijevic ever voicing those views, but I do remember very well that many opposition parties at that time tried to give -- throw doubt and suspicion on Mr. Kadijevic and that questions like that were asked of me and that later on in my book, and today also, I claim that Mr. Kadijevic always was and remains a Yugoslav --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kostic. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must endeavour to answer more directly and briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would like to ask you now something related to the Carrington Plan, and first of all I would like to put something to you from Exhibit 812 that the Prosecution provided in the case. We have this document only in English, Mr. Kostic, because it's a document provided and prepared by the European Union, and therefore it's only in English so it needs to be translated to you while I go through it. And it's a document on the Conference on Yugoslavia, a summary of the -- of the developments in that conference. And I quote from page 2, Your Honour, the fourth point. It says: "The fourth plenary session was held on 4 October 1991. The Chair concluded that all parties involved were breaching the cease-fire. With the exception of Serbia and Montenegro, all parties condemned the constitutional coup launched by Serbia in the collective Presidency. The Chair indicated that the EC and its Member States would not recognise the situation created which could only worsen institutional stalemate. "Slovenia and Croatia stressed that they would give effect to their declaration of independence from 7 October onwards ..." Were you present in that fourth plenary session, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present. I attended only sessions from the 18th of October and the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When such sessions took place, would you afterwards get information about how it went by your -- by these people that attended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were informed through the bulletins and the mass media as far as that goes, but I have it say that unfortunately Mr. Carrington and the leadership of The Hague conference attempted systematically to bypass the Presidency. So I couldn't testify here about what the 4th of October session dealt with. I can tell you what happened on the 18th of October and the 5th of November when I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me, nevertheless, put something to you from the 4th October because it's so important that you actually should know about it. It says here -- it's point 5, Your Honour, point 5. "In the margins of the fourth plenary, a meeting was held on the 4th of October chaired by the minister for foreign affairs of the Netherlands, assisted by Lord Carrington and Ambassador Wijnaendts, between the Croatian President Tudjman, and the Serbian President Milosevic, and the Minister of Defence General Kadijevic. A statement was read out subsequently by the Netherlands minister at a press conference, reflecting the agreement of the Yugoslav parties involved after Minister van den Broek had obtained the acquiescence of all Yugoslav parties present at the plenary meeting. This included the principle that a political solution should be sought on the basis of the perspective of recognition of the independence of those republics in Yugoslavia wishing it, and at the end of a negotiating process conducted in good faith and involving all parties.
