The recognition would be granted in the framework of a general settlement, and have the following components: "A loose association or alliance of sovereign or independent republics. "Adequate arrangements to be made for the protection of minorities, including human rights guarantees and possibly special status of certain area. "And no unilateral changes in borders." That is an agreement, at least according to this document, reached on the 4th of October, Mr. Kostic. Did you hear about this? Were you informed about this agreement by Mr. Milosevic or General Kadijevic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two questions in your question, actually; one concerning the truce that was concluded, whether on the 4th or on the 10th of October, and the second question that you put, I have to say it's quite unclear to me what was agreed at that session of the 4th of October. That was followed by the session of the 18th of October. At the session of the 18th of October, Mr. Milosevic objected to the document offered by Mr. Carrington and refused to accept it. He reminded Mr. Carrington that on the 4th of October, possible options had been discussed. The possible options were the ones listed in the document as well as the option for those republics that wished to do so to continue living in Yugoslavia and that they would have the same rights and be given the same treatment as the seceding republics. This option was missing from the document. At the session of the 18th, there was evidently a misunderstanding between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Carrington. In my book, which is in the tab, I wrote about this. Mr. Bulatovic later claimed that at the session of the 4th, The Hague document had been accepted by both Milosevic and Bulatovic. I don't know that, so there's nothing I can tell you about it. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds like a "Yes, I heard about it, and it's exactly as you've read out."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a pity we can't get these simple answers, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And actually, as you mentioned Mr. Bulatovic on this issue, I would like to actually quote now or to show to you a few excerpts from his book "Rules of Silence." Can this be please provided to everyone. I will first quote from what I think is in the B/C/S page 65. And actually, Mr. Bulatovic's understanding is exactly as Mr. Carrington's understanding of what was decided on the 4th of October. "Finally in a meeting in The Hague on 4th October, 1991, they -" and he refers here to Slobodan Milosevic and Tudjman - "accepted together with Lord Carrington and Hans van den Broek, chairman of the European Community Council of Ministers, a document indicating the road toward the adoption of an all-round agreement to solve the war crisis in the SFRY territories." And the solution he quotes as follows: "The basis of the solution, as the document said, will be: '... independence to those republics that want it at the end of the talks, which are to be held bona fide. The independence will be granted on the basis of a general solution and will consist of the following components: A loose association or association of independent and sovereign republics; adequate protection of human rights and a possible special status for some territories, but without any unilateral change of borders.'" So, Mr. Kostic, that's also Mr. Bulatovic's understanding that on the 4th of October, Mr. Milosevic, Tudjman, and everyone else present agreed to that. Can you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I? You haven't told me anything new. I read what Mr. Bulatovic wrote. I don't know if it's correct. I can only confirm that at the Assembly of Montenegro, Mr. Bulatovic stated that Mr. Milosevic had accepted this, and at the plenary Assembly of Montenegro, as the Presidency of the -- president of the Presidency of Montenegro, in his introductory expose, suggested that The Hague document be adopted. However, this was rejected by the Assembly. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would now like to continue with the book of Mr. Bulatovic. We have already mentioned a meeting in Belgrade on the 14th of October, 1991, and that's the meeting. I understand you were present. And on page 4 of the translation -- where would it be in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 66.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bulatovic writes the following about what was discussed and agreed: "They --" and I think he refers here to the Serbian leadership because it is related to the previous paragraph: "They hold the view that the status of the Serbian people in Croatia is an issue which has gained an international dimension and could be solved in its essence only as such. Until international mechanisms to protect the two Serbian Krajinas are found, one should maintain military balance with the existing forces and the achieved level of mobilisation of the JNA. They advocate demilitarisation -- demilitarising all areas in which inter-ethnic conflicts may break out. They especially have Bosnia and Herzegovina in mind. It is possible to achieve all of this with a radical peace proposal which they are expecting to see in the near future. They hope that Lord Carrington will shortly present a document stemming from an already-reached agreement." Do you recall this discussion and was it like this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall this discussion. I wrote about this discussion, which took place on the 14th, in my book. As for what Mr. Bulatovic wrote, I really don't remember it. I have to reiterate there are many things that are incorrect or invented in Mr. Momir Bulatovic's book. I drew attention to this in public and criticised it, but you keep referring to it. All I can say is here are the facts and here are the arguments put forward by both authors, so let's see what is correct. I even wrote down that neither Mr. Bulatovic nor Mr. Milosevic spoke much at this meeting, nor did they engage in much discussion of this very important issue. When Mr. Bulatovic and I clashed about the way to lift the siege of the barracks in Croatia, after Mr. Jovic's response, Mr. Mile Djukanovic stated that he had come to the meeting having the same opinion as me, but that after Mr. Jovic's response he was withdrawing this opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just one point that I actually asked you about. At that meeting on the 14th, could it be understood by everyone that an agreement was reached and that one -- that the Carrington Plan would be accepted? Could that be the impression of those present, including you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What meeting, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the 14th of October. The meeting of the 14th of October where Mr. Bulatovic actually wrote these things about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, had I had any such knowledge, had I known what Mr. Bulatovic states here, that a comprehensive solution would be found, I would not have been shortsighted enough to ask that 150.000 soldiers be mobilised and that the JNA go into offensive action and lift the siege of the barracks in Croatia. If I had known that a solution had been found, I would not have advocated this, madam. You seem to trust Mr. Bulatovic much more than you do me, but you would have more reason to quote from my book than his. However, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic describes in this section of the book also how the Assembly in Montenegro actually dealt with the proposal and that they discussed it in a positive sense and -- but we do not have to dwell on this. But I would quote from you and read from page 7 in the English, and Mr. Bulatovic is here speaking of the Montenegrin Assembly session held on the 17th October 1991, and he says the following in relation to that day: "I received information that Slobodan Milosevic needed to talk to me urgently." And I skip a few sentences, and then it says: "After several casual sentences, he told me that he had changed his position in relation to Lord Carrington's proposal and that he would reject the offered proposal at the plenary session in The Hague the following day. He advised me to do the same. When I realised what he was saying, I asked for more details. I wanted to know which crucial event had taken place in the meantime to change the decision, which as early as two days before I believed was rational, courageous and the only possible one. I was not given an answer, saying that the line that we were using was insecure. Slobodan told me that I need not know the details, just the decision and act accordingly." Mr. Kostic, my question to you is: What did happen that Mr. Milosevic changed his mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who said that, that he changed his behind?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just read to you what Mr. Bulatovic said, that Mr. Milosevic suddenly called him and had changed his mind, and my question to you is: Why did he change his mind? Why did he not stick to the agreement of the 4th October that was confirmed on the 14th of October according to Carrington and according to Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I repeat once again, there are many things that are incorrect in Momir Bulatovic's book "The Rules of Silence." He states that The Hague document was accepted by the Assembly of Montenegro. This is incorrect, and I deny this in my critique of his book. Don't expect me to assist you by testifying about a telephone conversation between Mr. Bulatovic and Mr. President Milosevic. I have to tell you that I have great reservations about everything Mr. Bulatovic writes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of any event, anything that might have happened that would explain the change of position on the part of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really not aware of any event that might have changed his mind. When we met at Batajnica on the morning of the 18th to fly to The Hague, Mr. Milosevic asked me what the position taken by the Assembly of Montenegro had been. I couldn't tell him because I had left the session early so that the Presidency take up a standpoint. He then told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see it's time. We have to stop, and we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just could I please tender this so that it is marked for identification, as we did with other passages of Mr. Bulatovic's book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about together 944. The earlier passages which were marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, 1 to 14, the English and the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. They're all marked for identification, yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
